text: Agent tutorial: a code review system on doeff agents, which drives a coding agent, here Claude Code, in a terminal session.
Here a scripted terminal plays Claude's screens, so the runs you see need no tmux, no Claude, and no login.
Step one: launch, watch until it ends, read the screen, stop.
launch session types the claude command, waits for the ready screen, and only then pastes the prompt.
monitor session reads the pane once a second. While the screen says esc to interrupt, the session is running.
At three seconds the shell prompt is back: the agent exited, a terminal status, so the loop ends.
capture output reads the review off the screen. Then stop session kills the session.
launch session is plain Python on top, and a doeff program underneath.
Before it opens a terminal, it yields effects. Is claude on the path? Where is home? Is there a login?
A handler answers each effect and resumes the program. Here an in-memory world answers; in production, the real system does.
In a world without a login, the same program raises at its check, and no terminal session is ever opened.
Step two. session scope stops the session on the way out of the with block.
When the review finishes, the block returns, and stop session runs.
When the timeout returns early from inside the loop, stop session still runs.
And when an exception leaves the block, stop session runs, and the error goes on to the caller.
Step three. on status change runs only when the status changes.
Eight polls, four changes: running, blocked, running again, and exited.
Blocked means the agent is waiting for input. Here it asks to run the tests, and the loop answers with send message.
The callback keeps the history, with the second of every change.
Step four. Many files at once, with asyncio and a limit.
A semaphore of two lets two reviews run. The next one starts when a slot frees up.
Four reviews take seven seconds, two at a time, and thirteen point one seconds, one at a time.
api finishes first, but gather returns the results in the order of the files.
Step five puts it together: a scope per session, callbacks for progress, a limited batch, and timeouts.
And under the session API, the driver is a doeff program: effects go out, and handlers send the answers back.
